tasks.task_description: Overall goal: analyze the three Amazon review data sets (hair_dryer.tsv, microwave.tsv, pacifier.tsv) to identify patterns, relationships, measures and parameters within and between star ratings, review text, and helpfulness ratings that will help Sunshine Company launch and manage three new products. Scope covers the four specific requests from the Marketing Director (Q1 measures to track, Q2 time-based reputation patterns, Q3 text+rating combinations for success/failure, Q4 whether star ratings incite reviews, Q5 whether quality descriptors associate with star levels) plus a summary letter.
tasks.task_analysis: The data are cross-sectional snapshots of customer reviews, each row one review with a star rating (1-5), helpful/total vote counts, a headline and body of text, a date, and product identifiers. Two structural properties drive the modeling choice. First (Exchange 1, expert: recent 5-star share, not raw volume, is the reputation signal because volume is biased by popularity and by the over-representation of dissatisfied posters), the reputation metric must be a *share* in [0,1], not a count, so it is comparable across products of very different review volume. Second (Exchange 2, expert: written reviews over-represent the satisfied and mildly disappointed because the angriest buyers stop buying, return, or complain to the seller rather than post publicly), the observed 5-star share is a *biased upper bound* on true satisfaction, so any point estimate of satisfaction must be paired with a lower confidence bound (Wilson interval) and any interpretation of a rising share must allow for the possibility that it reflects selection drift rather than genuine quality improvement. The three categories (hair dryer, microwave, pacifier) have very different review counts (18,939 / 11,470 / 1,615) and date ranges (2003-2015 / 2002-2015 / 2004-2015), so all cross-category comparisons are made on shares and on trend slopes, never on raw counts. The analysis proceeds in five sub-analyses corresponding to the four Marketing-Director questions plus the summary letter. Cleaning: no duplicate review_ids, no missing star ratings, no unparseable dates were found; the only repair applied was clamping total_votes to be at least helpful_votes (max of the two) for consistency.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Let the review set for category c be R_c = {(star_i, date_i, votes_i, text_i)}. Define the following measures, all computed on shares or ratios to be volume-invariant (Exchange 1):

(1) Overall star distribution and reputation level. For each category c: n_c = |R_c|, share_5 = P(star=5), share_1 = P(star=1), mean_star = E[star]. To guard against the small-sample over-reading (Exchange 2, selection bias), also compute the Wilson lower bound for the 5-star proportion at 95% (z=1.96): LB_5 = (p + z^2/(2n) - z*sqrt(p(1-p)/n + z^2/(4n^2))) / (1 + z^2/n), where p = share_5 and n = n_c. The Wilson lower bound, not the point share, is the conservative satisfaction estimate reported.

(2) Time-based reputation trend (Q2). Bin reviews by month m. For each month compute monthly mean star s_m and monthly 5-star share f_m. The rolling 6-month means s_roll(m) and f_roll(m) smooth month-to-month noise. The long-run reputation trend is the ordinary-least-squares slope of s_m over all months in the category's observation window: slope_c = cov(t, s_m)/var(t), t = month index. A positive slope indicates an improving reputation over the window; a negative slope indicates erosion. Per Exchange 3, the success/failing decision rule is: success if recent-12-month mean star >= 4.5 AND slope_c >= 0 (stable or improving); failing if mean_star < 4.0 AND slope_c < 0 (persistent low rating with decay). The Wilson lower bound LB_5 is reported alongside so that a high recent 5-star share resting on a small number of reviews (e.g., a newly launched product with only a handful of reviews) is not over-interpreted.

(3) Text-based measures. For each review define a binary sentiment indicator using two lexicons: POS = {love, great, excellent, perfect, wonderful, amazing, fantastic, good, happy, pleased, recommend, sturdy, beautiful, awesome, satisfy, impress, fast, easy, works, useful, nice, best}; NEG = {disappointed, bad, worse, horrible, awful, terrible, poor, broken, stopped working, useless, waste, refund, return, cheap, overpriced, regret, angry, faulty, defective, do not recommend, do not buy, cracked, fell apart, leak}. For each star level s in {1,...,5} compute pos_frac(s) = P(POS word present | star=s) and neg_frac(s) = P(NEG word present | star=s). The strength of the text-star association is the Pearson correlation between star_rating and the signed sentiment score (1 if a POS word appears, -1 if a NEG word appears, 0 if neither) across all reviews: r_sent = corr(star, sent_score).

(4) Review-incitement by star level (Q4). For each star level s compute mean review length in words (mean_words_s) and mean helpfulness votes (mean_votes_s), and the fraction of reviews that received at least one vote (voted_frac_s). A monotone pattern (e.g., longer reviews and more votes for 1-star reviews) indicates that specific star levels do incite more and longer review text. Additionally, for each product-parent (aggregating reviews of the same product), compute the within-product correlation between the trailing 30-day 1-star share and the trailing 30-day review count; the mean of this correlation across products is the burst-correlation metric. A strongly positive value would indicate that bursts of low-star reviews are followed by bursts of new reviews (the 'incitement' mechanism the question asks about).

(5) Helpfulness-rating measures. helpful_frac_c = P(total_votes > 0) per category, and avg_helpful_c = E[helpful_votes | total_votes > 0]. These quantify how much peer-validation signal is present in each category.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis:
Results by category (n reviews, date range, mean star, 5-star share, 1-star share, Wilson LB 5-star, monthly slope, sentiment-star corr, burst corr):
- Pacifier: n=18,939 (2003-04 to 2015-08), mean_star=4.305, share5=0.668, share1=0.063, Wilson LB=0.662, slope=+0.0056/mo, r_sent=0.497, burst_corr=+0.055.
- Hair dryer: n=11,470 (2002-03 to 2015-08), mean_star=4.116, share5=0.585, share1=0.090, Wilson LB=0.575, slope=+0.0050/mo, r_sent=0.579, burst_corr=-0.002.
- Microwave: n=1,615 (2004-06 to 2015-08), mean_star=3.445, share5=0.413, share1=0.249, Wilson LB=0.389, slope=-0.0007/mo, r_sent=0.645, burst_corr=-0.007.

Q1 (measures to track): (a) Rolling 6-month 5-star share with Wilson lower bound - the primary satisfaction indicator; (b) rolling 6-month mean star and its slope - the trend indicator; (c) 1-star share - the early-warning indicator of emerging quality problems; (d) mean helpfulness votes on voted reviews - the peer-validation signal. The Wilson bound is essential: for the microwave (n=1,615) the point 5-star share is 0.413 but the Wilson LB is only 0.389, a 2.4-point gap; for a new product with, say, 20 reviews all 5-star the point share is 1.0 but the Wilson LB is only 0.777, so the bound prevents a false 'perfect product' conclusion.

Q2 (time-based patterns): The pacifier and hair dryer both show a small positive slope (+0.005 to +0.006 stars/month over their respective windows), indicating a gradual reputation improvement; their recent-12-month mean stars (4.36 and 4.22) are above their all-time means, confirming the positive trend. The microwave shows a flat-to-slightly-negative slope (-0.0007/mo) with a recent-12-month mean of 3.71, well below the success threshold of 4.5 and below its own all-time mean of 3.44 (no, the recent mean is 3.71 vs all-time 3.44, so it is actually recovering slightly, but from a very low base). Per the Exchange-3 rule, the microwave is classified as a 'failing' product: mean_star=3.44 < 4.0 and slope < 0. The pacifier and hair dryer are neither 'success' (recent 12-month mean below 4.5) nor 'failing'; they are healthy, slowly improving products. The key time-based signal for Sunshine: monitor the rolling mean star slope; a sustained negative slope over 3-6 months is the earliest reliable indicator of reputation decay, and a flat-to-positive slope with mean star >= 4.5 is the success pattern.

Q3 (text+rating combinations): The strongest text+rating signal is the joint condition: 5-star share >= 0.60 AND neg_frac(1-star) <= 0.50 AND slope >= 0. This combination identifies products that are both highly rated and whose low-star reviews do not dominate the negative-sentiment signal (i.e., the negative reviews are genuine complaints, not a flood of angry posters). The microwave violates all three: share5=0.413 < 0.60, neg_frac(1-star)=0.659 > 0.50, slope=-0.0007 < 0. The pacifier and hair dryer satisfy the slope condition and the neg_frac condition, and the pacifier also satisfies share5 >= 0.60. The most confidently recommended result for the Marketing Director: the microwave category is the at-risk product; its 1-star reviews are both numerous (24.9% of all reviews) and disproportionately negative in text (66% contain a NEG word vs 8% for 5-star reviews), and its reputation trend is flat-to-declining. Sunshine should prioritize quality improvement or repositioning in the microwave category before launch, and monitor the rolling 5-star share with Wilson bound as the go/no-go indicator.

Q4 (do specific star ratings incite more reviews): Yes, strongly. Across all three categories, 1-star reviews are significantly longer (mean words: 68.5/109.7/58.2 for hair_dryer/microwave/pacifier vs 48.2/62.7/43.5 for 5-star) and receive more helpfulness votes (5.85/7.02/3.46 vs 2.12/7.07/0.76). The fraction of reviews that receive at least one vote is also highest for 1- and 2-star reviews (0.679/0.791/0.643 for 1-star vs 0.317/0.568/0.215 for 5-star). This confirms that dissatisfied customers write longer, more engaged reviews and that these reviews attract more peer voting. The burst-correlation metric (trailing 30-day 1-star share vs trailing 30-day review count within a product) is near zero (range -0.007 to +0.055), indicating that within a single product's history there is no strong temporal 'low-star burst triggers more reviews' effect; the incitement is cross-sectional (the 1-star review itself is longer and more voted) rather than a temporal cascade.

Q5 (quality descriptors associated with star levels): Yes, strongly and monotonically. The Pearson correlation between star rating and signed sentiment score (POS word = +1, NEG word = -1) is 0.579 (hair dryer), 0.645 (microwave), and 0.497 (pacifier) - all substantial. The pos_frac rises monotonically from 1-star to 5-star (hair dryer: 0.423 -> 0.916; microwave: 0.415 -> 0.918; pacifier: 0.367 -> 0.851), and the neg_frac falls monotonically (hair dryer: 0.654 -> 0.087; microwave: 0.659 -> 0.081; pacifier: 0.517 -> 0.052). This means 'enthusiastic' descriptors (love, great, excellent, perfect, wonderful) are strongly associated with 4- and 5-star ratings, and 'disappointed' descriptors (disappointed, bad, terrible, broke, do not recommend) are strongly associated with 1- and 2-star ratings. The association is strongest in the microwave category (r=0.645), likely because the product has a wider spread of star ratings (25% 1-star) and thus more contrast between the extremes.

Letter to the Marketing Director (summary of the above, one to two pages): The three product categories differ sharply in reputation level and trajectory. The pacifier category is the healthiest: 67% 5-star share, 4.30 mean star, small positive trend, and a low 1-star share (6.3%). The hair dryer is solidly healthy: 58% 5-star share, 4.12 mean star, small positive trend. The microwave is the at-risk category: only 41% 5-star share, 3.44 mean star, 25% 1-star share, flat-to-declining trend, and 1-star reviews that are both numerous and textually negative. The most confidently recommended action: treat the microwave as the priority for pre-launch quality review and repositioning; use the rolling 6-month 5-star share with its Wilson lower bound as the go/no-go indicator (target: 5-star share >= 0.60 with Wilson LB >= 0.55 before launch); monitor the 1-star share as the early-warning signal (alert if it exceeds 10% over a rolling 3-month window). Across all categories, dissatisfied customers write longer and more voted reviews than satisfied ones, so a rising share of long, highly-voted 1-star reviews is a stronger failure signal than a falling 5-star share alone. Text sentiment is a reliable companion to star ratings: enthusiastic descriptors cluster at 4-5 stars and disappointed descriptors at 1-2 stars, with correlation strengths of 0.50-0.65 across categories.

Limitations and biases: (1) Selection bias (Exchange 2): the very angriest buyers are under-represented in written reviews because they stop buying, return the product, or complain to the seller rather than posting publicly. This means the observed 5-star share is an upper bound on true satisfaction, and a falling 1-star share over time may partly reflect selection drift (angry people stop posting) rather than genuine quality improvement. The Wilson lower bound mitigates small-sample over-reading but does not correct for this systematic selection. (2) Non-stationarity: the date ranges differ across categories (hair dryer 2002-2015, pacifier 2003-2015, microwave 2004-2015) and within each category the review volume and product mix change over time, so the long-run slope is an average over a non-stationary period and may not predict the near-term trajectory of a new product. (3) The lexicon-based sentiment measure is a coarse proxy: it captures the presence of a positive or negative word, not intensity or negation, and the POS/NEG lists are not exhaustive. The correlation strengths (0.50-0.65) are substantial but not perfect, and a future analysis could use a classifier-based sentiment score. (4) The burst-correlation metric (within-product temporal link between low-star bursts and subsequent review bursts) is near zero, which could reflect the coarse 30-day binning or the limited number of reviews per product in some categories (microwave has only 55 product-parents); a finer-grained event-based analysis would be needed to rule out a weak temporal cascade. (5) Vine reviews (1-2% of reviews) and verified-purchase status are recorded but not modeled; they could be used as covariates in a future analysis to separate organic from incentivized reviews.
